metadata.title: CareerOS Computer Science MCQ Bank
notes: Imported from user-provided cs-questions minified banks.
Only valid single-answer MCQs were retained for current scoring compatibility.
Tests are deterministic and use weighted focus topics with mixed-topic coverage.

questions.prompt: Which notation is most commonly used to describe an upper bound on the growth rate of an algorithm?
questions.explanation: Big-O is used for asymptotic upper bounds.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search on an unsorted array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Linear search may need to inspect every element.

questions.prompt: Binary search requires the input collection to be:
options: Sorted according to the search key
Stored as a linked list only
questions.explanation: Binary search relies on sorted order to discard half the range.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order elements?
questions.explanation: Bubble sort compares adjacent pairs and swaps them when needed.

questions.prompt: What is the best-case time complexity of insertion sort on an already sorted array?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort performs a linear scan with no shifts in the sorted case.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm uses the divide-and-conquer idea of splitting an array into halves and merging sorted halves?
questions.explanation: Merge sort recursively sorts halves and merges them.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm selects the minimum remaining element and places it at the current position?
questions.explanation: Selection sort repeatedly chooses the minimum of the unsorted suffix.

questions.prompt: Breadth-first search explores a graph using which data structure in its standard iterative form?
questions.explanation: BFS uses a queue to explore vertices level by level.

questions.prompt: Depth-first search is naturally implemented using:
questions.explanation: DFS follows one branch deeply, matching stack behavior.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm is commonly used to find shortest paths in an unweighted graph?
questions.explanation: BFS computes shortest path distance in number of edges for unweighted graphs.

questions.prompt: A topological ordering exists only for which type of graph?
questions.explanation: Topological ordering is defined for DAGs.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea behind a greedy algorithm?
options: Make a locally best choice at each step
questions.explanation: Greedy algorithms build solutions through local choices.

questions.prompt: Dynamic programming is most useful when a problem has overlapping subproblems and:
questions.explanation: DP exploits overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.

questions.prompt: What prevents infinite recursion in a correctly designed recursive algorithm?
options: A larger input at every call
questions.explanation: A base case stops recursion.

questions.prompt: Which phase is typical in many divide-and-conquer algorithms?
options: Divide the problem into smaller subproblems
questions.explanation: Divide-and-conquer splits, solves, and combines subproblems.

questions.prompt: Kruskal's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by processing edges in what order?
questions.explanation: Kruskal's algorithm sorts edges by weight.

questions.prompt: Prim's algorithm grows a minimum spanning tree by repeatedly adding:
options: The cheapest edge crossing from the current tree to an outside vertex
The newest vertex's largest outgoing edge
questions.explanation: Prim's algorithm adds the minimum crossing edge.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm assumes edge weights are:
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy correctness requires no negative edge weights.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm can detect a reachable negative-weight cycle in a graph?
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford can detect negative cycles after relaxation.

questions.prompt: Naive string matching checks for a pattern by:
questions.explanation: The naive method compares the pattern at each possible starting position.

questions.prompt: If an algorithm does three independent passes over an array of size n, its time complexity is:
questions.explanation: Constant factors are ignored asymptotically; three passes are O(n).

questions.prompt: Which function grows fastest as n becomes large?
questions.explanation: Quadratic growth dominates linearithmic, linear, and logarithmic growth.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of accessing the middle element of an array when its index is known?
questions.explanation: Array indexing is constant time.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort?
questions.explanation: Merge sort has O(log n) levels and O(n) work per level.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm is not comparison-based in its common form?
questions.explanation: Counting sort uses counts of keys rather than pairwise comparisons.

questions.prompt: How many elements can binary search eliminate after one comparison in a sorted array?
questions.explanation: A comparison in binary search discards roughly half the remaining search space.

questions.prompt: In BFS from a source vertex, vertices at distance 1 are visited before vertices at distance:
questions.explanation: BFS visits by increasing number of edges from the source.

questions.prompt: In DFS, a vertex is usually marked visited when:
questions.explanation: Marking on discovery prevents repeated exploration.

questions.prompt: Memoization usually means:
options: Storing results of subproblems to avoid recomputation
questions.explanation: Memoization caches previously computed answers.

questions.prompt: Tabulation usually computes dynamic programming states:
questions.explanation: Tabulation fills a table from base cases upward.

questions.prompt: The activity-selection problem with finish times sorted is a classic example of:
questions.explanation: Choosing the earliest finishing compatible activity is a greedy strategy.

questions.prompt: The factorial recurrence n! = n * (n-1)! has the base case:
questions.explanation: By convention and recurrence consistency, 0! equals 1.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm is a classic divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm?
questions.explanation: Merge sort divides the array, sorts subarrays, and merges.

questions.prompt: Euclid's algorithm computes:
questions.explanation: Euclid's algorithm repeatedly uses remainders to compute the GCD.

questions.prompt: For a positive integer x, the expression x & 1 is commonly used to test whether x is:
questions.explanation: The least significant bit is 1 exactly for odd integers.

questions.prompt: A randomized algorithm may use:
questions.explanation: Randomized algorithms incorporate randomness.

questions.prompt: A loop invariant is a statement that is true:
options: Before and after each iteration of a loop
questions.explanation: Loop invariants help prove iterative algorithms correct.

questions.prompt: Backtracking solves problems by:
options: Building candidates and abandoning invalid partial candidates
questions.explanation: Backtracking explores choices and prunes infeasible branches.

questions.prompt: A polynomial-time algorithm has running time bounded by:
questions.explanation: Polynomial time is O(n^k) for constant k.

questions.prompt: In an undirected graph, a connected component is:
options: A maximal set of vertices connected by paths
questions.explanation: A connected component is maximal under reachability.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of a loop that runs from i = 1 to n and does O(1) work each iteration?
questions.explanation: The loop executes n times.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of two nested loops each running n times with O(1) work inside?
questions.explanation: The inner work executes n * n times.

questions.prompt: A stable sorting algorithm preserves:
options: The relative order of equal keys
questions.explanation: Stability preserves the order among records with equal keys.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm generally has O(n^2) worst-case time and O(1) extra space in its simple form?
questions.explanation: Simple selection sort is quadratic and in-place.

questions.prompt: If binary search fails to find an item, what has it determined?
options: The item is absent from the searched sorted range
The array was unsorted for sure
questions.explanation: Binary search proves absence from the considered sorted range.

questions.prompt: In the fractional knapsack problem, the standard greedy choice is to sort by:
questions.explanation: The fractional version is solved greedily by decreasing value density.

questions.prompt: The Fibonacci recurrence F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2) is often used to illustrate:
questions.explanation: The same Fibonacci subproblems recur many times in naive recursion.

questions.prompt: Which graph representation is usually better for sparse graphs?
options: Complete edge table with all nonedges
questions.explanation: Adjacency lists store only existing edges, which is efficient for sparse graphs.

questions.prompt: The time complexity of BFS using an adjacency list is:
questions.explanation: Each vertex and edge is processed a constant number of times.

questions.prompt: The time complexity of DFS using an adjacency list is:
questions.explanation: DFS visits vertices and scans adjacency lists.

questions.prompt: For an unweighted graph, BFS distance counts:
options: Number of edges in a shortest path
questions.explanation: In unweighted graphs, each edge has unit cost.

questions.prompt: A minimum spanning tree of a connected graph with V vertices contains exactly:
questions.explanation: Any tree on V vertices has V - 1 edges.

questions.prompt: The Longest Common Subsequence problem is commonly solved using:
questions.explanation: LCS has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.

questions.prompt: A recursive call should generally be made on:
options: A problem that makes progress toward a base case
questions.explanation: Progress toward a base case is necessary for termination.

questions.prompt: A proof of algorithm correctness should show:
options: That the algorithm terminates and returns the right result
questions.explanation: Correctness requires both termination and a valid result.

questions.prompt: Which one is usually considered faster for large n?
questions.explanation: Linear growth is asymptotically smaller than the others listed.

questions.prompt: Huffman coding builds an optimal prefix code by repeatedly combining:
questions.explanation: Huffman's greedy step combines the two smallest frequencies.

questions.prompt: A cycle in a directed graph is:
options: A path that starts and ends at the same vertex following edge directions
questions.explanation: Directed cycles must respect edge orientation.

questions.prompt: The comparison-sorting lower bound for worst-case sorting is:
questions.explanation: Comparison sorting has an information-theoretic lower bound of Omega(n log n).

questions.prompt: A brute-force algorithm usually means:
options: Trying straightforward possibilities without much optimization
questions.explanation: Brute force commonly enumerates possible solutions directly.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm is suitable for finding connected components in an undirected graph?
questions.explanation: Repeated DFS or BFS can mark each connected component.

questions.prompt: In DP, a state usually represents:
options: A subproblem whose answer is stored or computed
questions.explanation: DP states encode subproblems.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm transforms an array into a heap and repeatedly extracts the maximum or minimum?
questions.explanation: Heap sort uses heap construction and repeated extraction.

questions.prompt: Interpolation search is most appropriate when keys are:
options: Uniformly distributed in a sorted array
questions.explanation: Interpolation search estimates positions assuming fairly uniform distribution.

questions.prompt: The N-Queens problem is commonly solved using:
questions.explanation: N-Queens explores queen placements and backtracks on conflicts.

questions.prompt: Binary exponentiation is used to compute powers efficiently in:
questions.explanation: Exponentiation by squaring reduces the exponent by about half each step.

questions.prompt: For positive x, the expression x & (x - 1) clears:
options: The most significant digit in decimal
questions.explanation: Subtracting one flips bits through the least significant set bit; AND clears it.

questions.prompt: Randomized quicksort usually randomizes:
questions.explanation: Random pivot selection reduces dependence on input order.

questions.prompt: Amortized analysis studies:
options: Average cost over a sequence of operations
Only the cost of one random operation
questions.explanation: Amortized bounds distribute occasional expensive operations over many operations.

questions.prompt: Which design method is most directly associated with exploring all choices while pruning invalid partial solutions?
questions.explanation: Backtracking explores a search tree and prunes.

questions.prompt: A graph with no cycles and connected undirected structure is called:
questions.explanation: An undirected connected acyclic graph is a tree.

questions.prompt: A shortest path algorithm returns:
options: A path with minimum total cost under the chosen edge weights
A path with maximum number of edges always
questions.explanation: Shortest paths minimize path cost or distance.

questions.prompt: Edit distance between two strings can be computed with:
questions.explanation: Edit distance has standard DP transitions for insert, delete, and replace.

questions.prompt: An algorithm with O(1) extra space uses:
options: Constant additional memory independent of input size
questions.explanation: O(1) extra space means bounded auxiliary storage.

questions.prompt: Which expression is asymptotically equivalent to O(2n + 100)?
questions.explanation: Constants and lower-order fixed terms are ignored.

questions.prompt: Quick sort partitions an array around:
questions.explanation: Quicksort places elements relative to a pivot.

questions.prompt: Counting sort is efficient when:
options: The key range is not too large
All keys are strings of infinite length
questions.explanation: Counting sort depends on the range of key values.

questions.prompt: A greedy algorithm is correct only when:
options: Its local choices can be proven to lead to a global optimum
questions.explanation: Greedy correctness needs a proof such as exchange argument or matroid property.

questions.prompt: The Floyd-Warshall algorithm computes:
questions.explanation: Floyd-Warshall is a dynamic programming algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths.

questions.prompt: The input size for sorting n integers is usually measured primarily by:
questions.explanation: Sorting complexity is commonly expressed in terms of the element count n.
The loop variable doubles each time, so it runs about log2(n) iterations.
The outer loop runs n times and the inner loop runs O(log n) times.
The total iterations are n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = O(n^2).

questions.prompt: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) solves to:
questions.explanation: There are log n levels and O(n) work per level.

questions.prompt: The recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) solves to:
questions.explanation: The input halves until size 1, producing O(log n) calls.

questions.prompt: Which statement about quicksort is correct?
options: Its worst-case time is O(n log n) for every pivot rule
Its average time with good/random pivots is O(n log n)
It is stable in its standard in-place partition form
questions.explanation: Quicksort has average O(n log n), but worst case can be O(n^2).

questions.prompt: If quicksort always chooses the first element as pivot, which input often triggers worst-case behavior?
options: All elements hidden in a heap
Input length exactly power of two
questions.explanation: On sorted input, first-element pivot can create highly unbalanced partitions.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm is stable in its usual array-based implementation if the merge step breaks ties by taking from the left half first?
questions.explanation: Stable merge preserves equal-key order when ties choose the left item first.

questions.prompt: What is the main limitation of counting sort?
options: It requires a key range small enough to count efficiently
questions.explanation: Counting sort is efficient when the value range k is manageable.

questions.prompt: For radix sort on fixed-width integers with base b and d digits, the usual time complexity is:
questions.explanation: Radix sort performs d stable counting-like passes over n items plus base buckets.

questions.prompt: In a lower_bound binary search over sorted array a, what should the returned index represent?
options: The first index i such that a[i] >= target
The last index i such that a[i] <= target
Any index with the target only
questions.explanation: lower_bound returns the first position where the target could be inserted without violating order.

questions.prompt: Binary search over an answer space is valid when the predicate P(x) is:
questions.explanation: Parametric binary search needs a monotonic feasibility predicate.

questions.prompt: In interval scheduling, choosing the interval with earliest finishing time works because:
options: It leaves maximum remaining room for future intervals
It always chooses the longest interval
It sorts by starting time only
questions.explanation: The earliest-finish choice can be justified by an exchange argument.

questions.prompt: Which problem is NOT generally solved optimally by sorting items by value-to-weight ratio and taking whole items?
questions.explanation: The ratio greedy rule can fail for 0/1 knapsack because items are indivisible.

questions.prompt: In Huffman coding, why is a priority queue useful?
options: It repeatedly extracts the two minimum frequencies efficiently
questions.explanation: Huffman's greedy step repeatedly needs the two smallest nodes.

questions.prompt: The standard 0/1 knapsack DP state dp[i][w] usually represents:
options: Best value using first i items with capacity w
Shortest path from i to w
questions.explanation: The state captures a prefix of items and remaining/used capacity.

questions.prompt: For LCS of strings of lengths n and m, the classic DP time complexity is:
questions.explanation: The DP fills an n by m table of subproblems.

questions.prompt: In edit distance DP, the three classic operations are:
questions.explanation: Levenshtein distance uses insertion, deletion, and substitution/replacement.

questions.prompt: The LIS length can be found in O(n log n) using:
options: A tails array with binary search
questions.explanation: The tails method maintains minimum possible tail values and uses binary search.

questions.prompt: In matrix-chain multiplication DP, what is minimized?
options: Number of vertices in a graph
questions.explanation: Matrix-chain DP chooses parenthesization minimizing scalar multiplication count.

questions.prompt: In Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap and adjacency list, the common time complexity is:
questions.explanation: Each heap operation contributes logarithmic factors across vertices and edges.

questions.prompt: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail on some graphs with negative edges?
options: It finalizes a vertex before a later negative edge can improve it
questions.explanation: The greedy finalization property breaks when negative edges can reduce settled distances.

questions.prompt: Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges how many times to compute shortest paths without negative cycles?
questions.explanation: A shortest simple path has at most V - 1 edges.

questions.prompt: Floyd-Warshall has which standard time complexity for V vertices?
questions.explanation: It considers each intermediate vertex for every source-destination pair.

questions.prompt: A topological sort can be produced using Kahn's algorithm by repeatedly removing vertices with:
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm starts with sources of indegree zero.

questions.prompt: If Kahn's algorithm processes fewer than V vertices, the directed graph contains:
questions.explanation: Remaining vertices with nonzero indegree imply a directed cycle.

questions.prompt: In Kruskal's algorithm, a disjoint-set union structure is used mainly to:
options: Detect whether adding an edge creates a cycle
questions.explanation: DSU efficiently checks whether endpoints are already connected.

questions.prompt: If all edge weights in a connected graph are distinct, the MST is:
questions.explanation: Distinct weights imply a unique MST by cut/cycle properties.

questions.prompt: In an undirected graph, an edge is a bridge if removing it:
options: Increases the number of connected components
questions.explanation: A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects more of the graph.

questions.prompt: Tarjan's SCC algorithm uses low-link values to identify:
options: Strongly connected components in a directed graph
Minimum spanning trees in undirected graphs
questions.explanation: Low-link values help find roots of SCCs during DFS.

questions.prompt: In KMP, the prefix function or LPS array is used to:
options: Avoid rechecking characters after a mismatch
questions.explanation: KMP uses border information to shift the pattern efficiently.

questions.prompt: The Z-array value Z[i] for a string usually stores:
options: The length of the longest substring starting at i that matches the prefix
The number of distinct characters before i
questions.explanation: Z[i] measures prefix match length from position i.

questions.prompt: Rabin-Karp commonly uses:
questions.explanation: Rolling hashes allow efficient comparison of substring fingerprints.

questions.prompt: Randomized quicksort has expected O(n log n) time because:
options: The pivot is unlikely to be consistently terrible
It compares each pair exactly once always
questions.explanation: Random pivots make persistently unbalanced partitions unlikely.

questions.prompt: If a dynamic array doubles its capacity when full, append has:
options: O(n) amortized time for every operation
questions.explanation: Expensive copies are spread over many cheap appends.

questions.prompt: The closest-pair-of-points divide-and-conquer algorithm achieves O(n log n) mainly by:
options: Checking only a constant number of candidates in the merge strip after sorting
Trying every pair in both halves
questions.explanation: The strip check is bounded after sorting by y-coordinate.

questions.prompt: The orientation test for three points is commonly based on:
options: The sign of a cross product
The sign of a hash value
The length of a DFS stack
questions.explanation: The 2D cross product indicates clockwise, counterclockwise, or collinear order.

questions.prompt: The sieve of Eratosthenes computes primes up to n in roughly:
questions.explanation: The classical sieve runs in O(n log log n).

questions.prompt: Fast modular exponentiation usually reduces the exponent by:
options: Converting the base to a graph
questions.explanation: Binary exponentiation repeatedly squares and halves the exponent.

questions.prompt: A common way to enumerate all submasks of mask is:
questions.explanation: The expression (s - 1) & mask walks through submasks efficiently.
The outer loop is O(n), and the inner loop is O(log n).

questions.prompt: The recurrence T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) solves to:
questions.explanation: By the Master Theorem, n^log2(3) dominates the linear combine work.

questions.prompt: The recurrence T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) solves to:
questions.explanation: Here a = 4, b = 2, so n^log_b(a) = n^2 dominates.

questions.prompt: Which condition makes insertion sort attractive despite its O(n^2) worst case?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort is adaptive and fast on nearly sorted data.

questions.prompt: Which statement about heap sort is correct?
options: It is in-place in its standard array implementation
questions.explanation: Heap sort usually uses O(1) extra array space and O(n log n) time.

questions.prompt: Why is merge sort often preferred for linked lists?
options: Merging linked lists can be done without random access
It requires indexing into the middle in O(1) always
questions.explanation: Linked lists support efficient pointer-based merging.

questions.prompt: Which statement about stable sorting is correct?
options: Stable sort matters when records have secondary information beyond the key
Stable sort means sorted in descending order only
questions.explanation: Stability preserves ordering among equal keys, useful for multi-key sorting.

questions.prompt: When searching for the first true value in a boolean monotonic array F F F T T, binary search should bias toward:
options: The left half after finding true
The right half after finding true
questions.explanation: To find the first true, continue searching left after a true.

questions.prompt: If a rotated sorted array contains no duplicates, which strategy can find a target in O(log n)?
options: At each step identify which half is sorted
Sort the array first using bubble sort
questions.explanation: One half remains sorted; this property guides binary search.

questions.prompt: The cut property in MST algorithms says that the lightest edge crossing any cut is:
options: Safe to add to some MST
Always the heaviest edge in every cycle
questions.explanation: The lightest edge crossing a cut is safe for MST construction.

questions.prompt: For scheduling to minimize maximum lateness on a single machine, the classic greedy order is:
questions.explanation: Earliest due date order minimizes maximum lateness in the standard setting.

questions.prompt: In coin change for minimum number of coins with unlimited coins, a typical transition is:
questions.explanation: Taking a coin reduces the amount by that coin value.

questions.prompt: For counting combinations in unbounded coin change, why is coin loop usually outside the amount loop?
options: To avoid counting different orders as distinct combinations
questions.explanation: Loop ordering controls whether permutations or combinations are counted.

questions.prompt: In longest palindromic subsequence DP, when s[i] == s[j], the typical recurrence uses:
questions.explanation: Matching ends can wrap an optimal subsequence inside.

questions.prompt: A DP can be space-optimized when:
options: Each state depends only on a small number of previous layers
It uses all future rows arbitrarily
questions.explanation: Limited dependencies allow rolling arrays or compressed storage.

questions.prompt: In a DAG, shortest paths can be computed efficiently by:
options: Sorting vertex labels by ASCII only
Using bubble sort on edge names
questions.explanation: Topological order ensures each predecessor is processed before successors.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm is used to find articulation points in an undirected graph?
options: DFS with discovery times and low values
questions.explanation: Articulation points can be found using DFS low-link analysis.

questions.prompt: In an undirected graph, a non-root DFS vertex u is an articulation point if it has a child v such that:
questions.explanation: If no back edge from v's subtree reaches above u, removing u separates the graph.

questions.prompt: The condensation graph of strongly connected components is always:
questions.explanation: Collapsing SCCs removes directed cycles between components.

questions.prompt: In Kosaraju's algorithm, the second DFS is run on:
options: The transposed graph in decreasing finish-time order
The original graph in random order
A sorted list of weights only
questions.explanation: Kosaraju uses finish order from the original graph and DFS on the transpose.

questions.prompt: Which statement about bipartite checking is correct?
options: It can be done by BFS or DFS two-coloring
It is impossible for disconnected graphs
It only works for weighted graphs
questions.explanation: A graph is bipartite iff it can be colored with two colors without conflict.

questions.prompt: A graph is not bipartite if BFS two-coloring finds:
options: An edge connecting vertices of the same color
questions.explanation: Same-color endpoints violate bipartite coloring.

questions.prompt: Which max-flow algorithm repeatedly finds augmenting paths in the residual graph?
questions.explanation: Ford-Fulkerson augments flow along residual paths.

questions.prompt: In the Edmonds-Karp algorithm, augmenting paths are chosen using:
questions.explanation: Edmonds-Karp uses shortest augmenting paths in edge count via BFS.

questions.prompt: If two substrings have different rolling hash values under the same hash function, then:
questions.explanation: Equal strings must hash equally; unequal hashes prove inequality.

questions.prompt: If two substrings have equal rolling hash values under a modular hash, then:
options: They may still be different due to collision
They are guaranteed identical in all cases
One is necessarily a prefix of the other
questions.explanation: Hash collisions are possible unless using a collision-free representation.

questions.prompt: In randomized selection, expected linear time comes from:
options: Random pivot partitioning around the desired rank
Sorting the full array every time
Using a heap for all elements always
questions.explanation: Quickselect discards one partition and random pivots yield expected linear work.

questions.prompt: Path compression plus union by rank in DSU gives amortized time per operation of approximately:
questions.explanation: The inverse Ackermann function alpha(n) grows extremely slowly.

questions.prompt: For subset DP over all masks of n elements, the number of masks is:
questions.explanation: Each of n elements is either in or out of a subset.

questions.prompt: The DP transition dp[mask] often uses mask without one element. This is commonly computed by:
options: mask ^ (1 << i) when bit i is set
questions.explanation: XOR removes a set bit when that bit is known to be present.

questions.prompt: A 2-approximation algorithm for a minimization problem guarantees a solution cost:
options: At most twice the optimal cost
At least twice the optimal cost
questions.explanation: For minimization, ratio 2 means cost <= 2 * OPT.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes NP?
options: Decision problems whose yes certificates can be verified in polynomial time
Problems requiring O(n!) time by definition
questions.explanation: NP is defined by polynomial-time verifiability of certificates.

questions.prompt: To prove a problem X is NP-hard, a standard approach is to:
options: Reduce a known NP-hard problem to X in polynomial time
Reduce X to a trivial problem only
questions.explanation: If a known hard problem reduces to X, then X is at least as hard.

questions.prompt: An exchange argument most commonly proves correctness of:
questions.explanation: Exchange arguments show an optimal solution can be transformed to include greedy choices.

questions.prompt: For a loop invariant proof, which three parts are usually shown?
questions.explanation: Loop invariant proofs establish truth before, during, and after the loop.

questions.prompt: Tail recursion means:
options: The recursive call is the last operation in the function
The function has two recursive calls
The input is a linked list
questions.explanation: In tail recursion, no work remains after the recursive call returns.

questions.prompt: Branch and bound differs from plain backtracking mainly by:
options: Using bounds to prune search branches that cannot beat the best solution
questions.explanation: Bounds rule out parts of the search tree that cannot improve the incumbent.

questions.prompt: Meet-in-the-middle is useful when brute force over n items is too large but:
options: Splitting into two halves gives about 2^(n/2) work per side
questions.explanation: Meet-in-the-middle trades 2^n enumeration for two smaller half enumerations.

questions.prompt: If an algorithm first sorts n items and then scans them once, the total time is:
questions.explanation: The O(n log n) sort dominates the O(n) scan.

questions.prompt: What is the asymptotic solution of T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + O(n)?
questions.explanation: Each level contributes O(n) total work and the recursion depth is O(log n).

questions.prompt: What is the asymptotic solution of T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n / log n), ignoring low-level constant issues?
questions.explanation: The recursion tree sums roughly n * (1/log n + 1/(log n - 1) + ...), giving O(n log log n).

questions.prompt: The recurrence T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) has growth closest to:
questions.explanation: It follows Fibonacci-like exponential growth.
The inner loop runs floor(n/i) times, so the total is n * H_n = O(n log n).
The total is sum_{i=1}^n O(log i) = O(n log n).

questions.prompt: What is the exact worst-case number of comparisons made by standard binary insertion position search for inserting one item into a sorted array of length n?
questions.explanation: Finding one insertion position among n+1 gaps requires ceil(log2(n+1)) comparisons in the worst case.

questions.prompt: In introsort, the algorithm usually switches from quicksort to heapsort when:
options: The recursion depth becomes too large
questions.explanation: Introsort limits quicksort's worst case by switching to heapsort after excessive depth.

questions.prompt: Which input is most dangerous for naive quicksort that chooses the last element as pivot and partitions with <= on every comparison?
options: Already sorted or reverse sorted array
Array of random unique values only
questions.explanation: Extreme pivots repeatedly produce unbalanced partitions.

questions.prompt: The Dutch National Flag partitioning is especially useful in quicksort when:
options: The array has many duplicate keys
All keys are floating point NaN only
questions.explanation: Three-way partitioning groups less-than, equal-to, and greater-than pivot values.

questions.prompt: Median-of-medians selection guarantees:
options: Worst-case O(n log n) selection only
questions.explanation: The median-of-medians pivot ensures a constant fraction is discarded each step.

questions.prompt:

questions.prompt: Which property makes ordinary array indexing constant time?
options: The elements are stored in contiguous memory and have a fixed element size
The array stores a hash table for every index
Every element stores a pointer to the next element
questions.explanation: An address can be computed as base plus index times element size.

questions.prompt: For a zero-indexed array of length n, which index refers to the last element?
questions.explanation: Zero-indexed arrays use positions 0 through n - 1.

questions.prompt: What is the usual time complexity of reading A[i] from a valid index in an array?
questions.explanation: Direct indexing does not scan earlier elements.

questions.prompt: Which operation is usually costly on a plain fixed array because elements may need shifting?
options: Inserting a new element at the beginning
Replacing an element at a known index
Computing the length stored in metadata
questions.explanation: Insertion at the front moves all existing elements one position to the right.

questions.prompt: If an int array stores 4-byte integers and starts at address 1000, what address stores A[3]?
questions.explanation: The address is 1000 + 3 * 4 = 1012.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a static array?
options: Its capacity is fixed after allocation
It expands automatically on every insertion
It must use pointers between consecutive elements
questions.explanation: A static array has a fixed amount of storage.

questions.prompt: What is the space complexity of storing n values in an array?
questions.explanation: The storage grows linearly with the number of elements.

questions.prompt: Which data structure commonly uses a contiguous buffer underneath?
questions.explanation: A dynamic array maintains a resizable contiguous buffer.

questions.prompt: What does each node in a singly linked list normally contain?
options: A complete copy of the list
Two child pointers named left and right
A value and a reference to the next node
questions.explanation: A singly linked node links forward to the next node.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of inserting at the head of a singly linked list when the new node is available?
questions.explanation: Only the new node pointer and head pointer need updates.

questions.prompt: Why is random access slow in a linked list?
options: Each node stores all possible indices
Nodes must be followed one by one from a known starting point
questions.explanation: A linked list does not provide address arithmetic for index lookup.

questions.prompt: Which extra pointer distinguishes a doubly linked list node from a singly linked list node?
questions.explanation: Doubly linked nodes link both forward and backward.

questions.prompt: Which pointer update is essential when deleting the first node of a singly linked list?
options: Move the head pointer to the second node
Move the tail pointer to NULL always
questions.explanation: The head must no longer refer to the removed node.

questions.prompt: What does the tail pointer usually store in a linked list implementation?
options: A reference to the last node
A pointer to the smallest value always
questions.explanation: A tail pointer makes operations at the end easier.

questions.prompt: Which traversal pattern is natural for a singly linked list?
options: Jump directly to index i in O(1)
questions.explanation: The list is traversed by repeatedly moving to the next node.

questions.prompt: What does an empty linked list head usually contain?
options: NULL or an equivalent null reference
The address of the last removed node
questions.explanation: A null head commonly represents no first node.

questions.prompt: Which access rule defines a stack?
questions.explanation: A stack removes the most recently inserted item first.

questions.prompt: What is the usual name of the stack insertion operation?
questions.explanation: push adds an item to the top of a stack.

questions.prompt: What is the usual name of the stack removal operation?
questions.explanation: pop removes the top item.

questions.prompt: Which operation reads the top item without removing it?
questions.explanation: peek or top inspects the next item to be popped.

questions.prompt: Which structure is the standard helper for checking balanced parentheses?
questions.explanation: Opening brackets can be pushed and matched against later closing brackets.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of push in a linked-list stack when memory allocation is treated as O(1)?
questions.explanation: A new node can be added at the head in constant time.

questions.prompt: What problem occurs when popping from an empty stack?
questions.explanation: Underflow means attempting to remove an item that is not present.

questions.prompt: Which expression notation is naturally evaluated using a stack from left to right?
questions.explanation: Postfix evaluation pushes operands and applies operators to stack values.

questions.prompt: Which access rule defines a basic queue?
questions.explanation: A queue removes the oldest inserted item first.

questions.prompt: What is the usual queue operation that inserts an element at the rear?
questions.explanation: enqueue adds an item to the back of the queue.

questions.prompt: What is the usual queue operation that removes an element from the front?

questions.prompt: Which implementation avoids shifting all elements on every dequeue from an array-based queue?

questions.prompt: What does a deque allow that a simple queue does not?

questions.prompt: In a circular queue, what usually happens when the rear index reaches the physical end of the array?
options: It deletes the front element automatically
It wraps around to the beginning if space exists
questions.explanation: Modulo arithmetic can reuse freed positions at the front.

questions.prompt: Which condition often indicates an empty circular queue when size is explicitly stored?
options: front is always greater than rear
questions.explanation: The size field cleanly distinguishes empty from full.

questions.prompt: Which scheduling policy is most directly modeled by a FIFO queue?
questions.explanation: FIFO serves requests in arrival order.

questions.prompt: What is the topmost node of a rooted tree called?
questions.explanation: The root has no parent in a rooted tree.

questions.prompt: What is a leaf node?
options: A node with exactly two children
A node that stores the largest value
questions.explanation: Leaves are terminal nodes.

questions.prompt: What is the parent of a node in a rooted tree?
options: Any node at the same depth
The node with the largest key
The node directly above it on the path to the root
questions.explanation: A parent is the immediate predecessor toward the root.

questions.prompt: Which traversal visits root, then left subtree, then right subtree in a binary tree?
questions.explanation: Preorder processes the root before its children.

questions.prompt: Which traversal visits nodes level by level from the root?
questions.explanation: Breadth-first traversal uses increasing depth order.

questions.prompt: What is the height of a tree commonly measured as?
options: The number of siblings of the root
The smallest key minus the largest key
The length of the longest downward path from root to a leaf
The number of null pointers only
questions.explanation: Height captures the deepest root-to-leaf distance.

questions.prompt: In a binary tree, how many children can a node have at most?
questions.explanation: Binary means at most two children per node.

questions.prompt: Which structure is naturally used to implement breadth-first traversal of a tree?
questions.explanation: A queue stores nodes in discovery order by level.

questions.prompt: What ordering rule defines a standard binary search tree with unique keys?
options: The root must always store the smallest key
All leaves must be at the same depth
Children must be inserted from left to right only
Keys in the left subtree are smaller and keys in the right subtree are larger
questions.explanation: The BST property partitions keys around each node.

questions.prompt: Which traversal of a binary search tree outputs keys in sorted order?
questions.explanation: Inorder visits left subtree, node, then right subtree.

questions.prompt: What is the average search time in a reasonably balanced BST with n nodes?
questions.explanation: A balanced tree reduces the search space by roughly half each level.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case height of an unbalanced BST with n nodes?
questions.explanation: Sorted insertions can create a chain.

questions.prompt: Where is the minimum key found in a non-empty BST?
questions.explanation: Following left links leads to smaller keys until no smaller child exists.

questions.prompt: Where is the maximum key found in a non-empty BST?
options: At the first inserted node always
questions.explanation: Following right links leads to larger keys.

questions.prompt: When deleting a BST node with two children, which replacement is commonly used?
options: The root of an unrelated tree
Its inorder successor or inorder predecessor
The median of an external array only
questions.explanation: Successor or predecessor preserves the BST ordering property.

questions.prompt: Which input order can make a plain BST highly skewed?
questions.explanation: Inserting sorted keys into a naive BST can produce a linked-list shape.

questions.prompt: Which property must a min-heap satisfy?
options: Every left child is less than every right child
Every parent key is less than or equal to its children
The root stores the largest key
questions.explanation: The minimum key is kept at the root by the heap-order property.

questions.prompt: Where is the minimum element in a binary min-heap?
questions.explanation: The root is no larger than any child, so it holds the minimum.

questions.prompt: Which operation removes the top-priority item from a priority queue?
options: extract-min or extract-max depending on priority direction
questions.explanation: Extraction removes the item with highest priority according to the queue ordering.

questions.prompt: In an array representation of a zero-indexed binary heap, what is the parent index of child i > 0?
questions.explanation: The parent formula reverses the child formulas.

questions.prompt: What is the usual time complexity of insert into a binary heap?

questions.prompt: What is the usual time complexity of finding the minimum in a min-heap without removing it?
questions.explanation: The minimum is stored at the root.

questions.prompt: Which shape property does a binary heap maintain?
options: It is always a perfect binary tree
It is a linked list sorted by priority
It is a complete binary tree
It is always a binary search tree
questions.explanation: Binary heaps are complete trees filled level by level.

questions.prompt: Which operation restores heap order after moving a leaf upward?
questions.explanation: Sift up repeatedly swaps with the parent when heap order is violated.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea behind a hash table?
options: Use tree rotations for every lookup
Store keys only in sorted linked order
Scan all keys for every query by design
Use a hash function to map keys to bucket positions

questions.prompt: What is a collision in a hash table?
options: A key is larger than the table size
Two different keys map to the same bucket or slot
questions.explanation: Collisions occur because many possible keys map into limited table positions.

questions.prompt: What is the expected average lookup time of a well-sized hash table?
questions.explanation: With a good hash function and controlled load, expected lookup is constant time.

questions.prompt: Which collision handling method stores multiple colliding keys in a bucket list or similar container?
questions.explanation: Separate chaining keeps a collection of keys per bucket.

questions.prompt: Which collision handling method searches alternative table slots inside the array itself?
questions.explanation: Open addressing probes within the table for an available slot.

questions.prompt: What does the load factor of a hash table roughly measure?
options: The ratio of stored entries to table capacity
The number of child pointers per node
questions.explanation: Load factor is commonly n divided by m.

questions.prompt: Why do hash tables often resize?
options: To convert all keys to strings
To remove the need for equality checks
To keep the load factor within a useful range
questions.explanation: Too high a load factor increases collisions and probe lengths.

questions.prompt: Which property is required for equal keys in a correct hash table?
options: Equal keys must have random hash values each lookup
Equal keys must occupy different tables
Equal keys must hash consistently to the same hash value
Equal keys must never be compared

questions.prompt: What is a graph made of?
questions.explanation: Graphs model entities as vertices and relationships as edges.

questions.prompt: In an undirected graph, what does an edge between u and v imply?
options: The edge must have negative weight
The connection can be used in both directions

questions.prompt: Which graph representation uses a square table to record whether pairs of vertices are adjacent?

questions.prompt: Which graph representation stores a list of neighbors for each vertex?

questions.prompt: Which traversal explores neighbors level by level from a starting vertex?

questions.prompt: What is the degree of a vertex in an undirected graph?

questions.prompt: What does a weighted graph edge store in addition to endpoints?

questions.prompt: What does a trie primarily store efficiently?

questions.prompt: In a trie storing lowercase English words, what does each level commonly represent?

questions.prompt: Which operation asks whether a set contains a given element?

questions.prompt: What abstract data type stores key-value pairs?

questions.prompt: What is a common way to implement a set for average O(1) lookup?

questions.prompt: What is a common way to implement an ordered map?

questions.prompt: What is the role of a terminal marker in a trie?

It stores the root height only

questions.prompt: Which structure is better suited for prefix search among words?

questions.prompt: A dynamic array doubles capacity whenever it is full. What is the amortized cost of append?

questions.prompt: Why is growing a dynamic array by exactly one slot on every full append bad?

It converts the array into a linked list

questions.prompt: Which shrink policy helps avoid resize thrashing in a dynamic array?
options: Shrink only when size falls far below capacity, such as one-quarter full

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time of a single append to a full dynamic array that must resize?

questions.prompt: Which operation remains O(1) on a dynamic array if the index is known and valid?

Delete from the middle without shifting

questions.prompt: What is a common reason dynamic arrays have better iteration speed than linked lists?

questions.prompt: If a dynamic array has size 17 and capacity 32, what is its load relative to capacity?

questions.prompt: Which statement about reserving capacity in a dynamic array is most accurate?
options: It can reduce future reallocations when the approximate final size is known
It changes indexed access from O(n) to O(1)
It makes deletion from the middle O(1) without side effects

The deleted node stores all predecessor pointers
The head pointer is never changed
The previous node's next pointer must bypass the deleted node

All old nodes must be reversed
The new node must have two children

The number of stored values to zero

By comparing node values to zero only
By checking whether the current node is back at the starting node

The tail with next set to NULL

questions.prompt: In a complete binary tree with n nodes, what is the height asymptotically?

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of nodes at level k of a binary tree if the root is level 0?

questions.prompt: Which traversal is usually implemented with a queue for binary trees?

The root is the only node
Keys are stored in sorted array order
Every node has only one child

questions.prompt: Which traversal can be done in O(1) extra space by temporarily modifying right pointers and restoring them?

Restore balance while preserving inorder key order

questions.prompt: In an AVL tree, what quantity is tightly bounded at every node?

The hash value of every key
The degree of every graph vertex
The height difference between left and right subtrees

questions.prompt: What is the search complexity of a red-black tree with n nodes?

questions.prompt: Which operation can cause a self-balancing BST to perform rotations?

Counting the capacity of an array

questions.prompt: What does an order-statistic tree store in addition to ordinary BST links?

questions.prompt: Why are balanced trees preferred over plain BSTs for adversarial insertion orders?

questions.prompt: What does a tree rotation preserve?

The exact parent of every node
The array index of every node

Every key is stored in a linked child pointer

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a tombstone in open addressing deletion?

Store the root of a tree

questions.prompt: What happens to expected probe lengths as open addressing load factor approaches 1?

questions.prompt: Which probing strategy uses h(k), h(k)+1, h(k)+2 and so on modulo table size?

questions.prompt: Which strategy uses a second hash function to determine the probe step?

questions.prompt: In separate chaining, what mostly determines average bucket length?

Tree height of an unrelated BST

questions.prompt: Why should a hash table compare keys after finding a matching hash or bucket?

questions.prompt: What is rehashing?

questions.prompt: For a dense graph with V vertices, what is the space usage of an adjacency matrix?

questions.prompt: Which representation tests whether edge (u, v) exists in O(1) time for unweighted graphs?

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of BFS using adjacency lists on a graph with V vertices and E edges?

questions.prompt: What extra structure is usually used to avoid revisiting vertices in graph traversal?

questions.prompt: Which representation is most compact for algorithms that process edges as a simple list of triples?

questions.prompt: What is a self-loop in a graph?

An edge from a vertex to itself

questions.prompt: What abstract operation does find(x) perform in a disjoint set union structure?

questions.prompt: What does union(a, b) do in DSU?

Keep every tree perfectly sorted by key

questions.prompt: What is union by rank or size meant to prevent?

questions.prompt: Which graph concept is DSU especially good at maintaining in an undirected graph with edge additions?

Topological order of a directed cycle

Whether adding an edge would connect vertices already in the same component

To link each element toward its set representative

a and b are stored in adjacent array cells
a must be the root of a binary tree

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of point update and prefix sum query in a Fenwick tree with n elements?

questions.prompt: What is a segment tree commonly used for?

questions.prompt: What does lazy propagation in a segment tree postpone?

questions.prompt: What is the usual space complexity of an array-based segment tree?

questions.prompt: Which query is naturally answered in O(1) by a sparse table after O(n log n) preprocessing for idempotent operations?

questions.prompt: Which data structure would you choose for many point updates and range sum queries on an array?

questions.prompt: In a segment tree, what does each internal node usually represent?

questions.prompt: Which two structures are typically combined to implement an O(1) LRU cache?

questions.prompt: Which structure can answer k-th smallest queries when a BST is augmented with subtree sizes?

questions.prompt: Which structure represents sets with possible false positives but no false negatives?
questions.explanation: A Bloom filter uses multiple hashes into a bit array.

questions.prompt: A dynamic array grows by factor 2 and shrinks only when one-quarter full. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The policy makes middle insertion O(1) worst-case
The array can never have unused capacity
Append and pop can be O(1) amortized while avoiding immediate grow-shrink thrashing
Every append becomes O(log n) worst-case
questions.explanation: The gap between grow and shrink thresholds provides hysteresis.

questions.prompt: A queue is implemented with two stacks, transferring all items only when the output stack is empty. What is the amortized dequeue cost?
questions.explanation: Each element moves from input stack to output stack at most once before being removed.

questions.prompt: In a partially persistent data structure, what is allowed?
options: Only the current version can be queried
All versions are deleted after every update
Updates to every old version with no extra metadata
Queries on old versions and updates only to the newest version
questions.explanation: Partial persistence preserves past versions for reading but updates the latest version.

questions.prompt: What is path copying in persistent trees?
options: Hashing every node into a queue
Copying nodes along the updated root-to-leaf path while sharing unchanged subtrees
Copying the entire tree for every query
Deleting the old root after every update
questions.explanation: Only nodes affected by the update path need new versions.

questions.prompt: What is the amortized time of DSU operations with union by rank and path compression?
options: Inverse-Ackermann time per operation, effectively constant
questions.explanation: The theoretical bound is O(alpha(n)) per operation over a sequence.

questions.prompt: Why is the potential method used in data structure analysis?
options: To store graph vertices in sorted order
To prove amortized bounds by tracking stored credit in the state
To guarantee no operation ever takes more than O(1)
questions.explanation: Potential accounts for future work paid for by previous cheap operations.

questions.prompt: Which heap has O(1) amortized decrease-key but O(log n) amortized delete-min?
questions.explanation: Fibonacci heaps defer consolidation to achieve cheap decrease-key.

questions.prompt: What makes a purely functional persistent stack efficient?
options: push and pop can share tail nodes between versions
Every operation must copy all nodes
questions.explanation: A stack node can point to an older tail without mutation.

questions.prompt: In an AVL tree, which imbalance case is fixed by a left rotation on the left child followed by a right rotation on the node?
questions.explanation: A left-right imbalance first converts to a left-left shape, then rotates right.

questions.prompt: In a red-black tree, what does equal black-height mean?
options: Every path from a node to descendant NIL leaves has the same number of black nodes
The root must have exactly two red children
Every path has the same number of red nodes
questions.explanation: Black-height is a core red-black invariant.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum asymptotic height of a red-black tree with n internal nodes?
questions.explanation: Red-black coloring rules prevent paths from being more than a constant factor apart.

questions.prompt: In a treap, if priorities are random and independent, what is the expected height?
questions.explanation: A random-priority treap has the same shape distribution as a random BST.

questions.prompt: What is the amortized complexity of splay tree search?
questions.explanation: Individual accesses can be linear, but amortized access is logarithmic.

questions.prompt: What extra field lets a balanced BST answer rank(key) efficiently?
questions.explanation: Rank is computed from sizes of skipped left subtrees.

questions.prompt: Which operation is naturally supported by treaps using split and merge?
options: Insert or delete by splitting around a key and merging pieces
questions.explanation: Treap split/merge preserve both BST and heap priority invariants.

questions.prompt: Why are rotations in augmented balanced trees delicate?
options: Rotations are forbidden in balanced trees
Auxiliary fields such as heights or subtree sizes must be recomputed correctly
questions.explanation: The structural change affects metadata on rotated nodes.

questions.prompt: Why are B-trees used for disks and databases?
options: They store every key in a separate disk file
They eliminate the need for sorted order
They have high branching factor, reducing the number of block reads
questions.explanation: A B-tree node is sized to a disk or cache block and stores many keys.

questions.prompt: In a B-tree of minimum degree t, what is the maximum number of keys in a non-root node?
questions.explanation: A B-tree node has between t - 1 and 2t - 1 keys except for special root cases.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a B+ tree from a classic B-tree in many database indexes?
options: It can have only two children per node
Records or record pointers are stored at leaves, and leaves are linked for scans
questions.explanation: B+ tree internal nodes guide search while leaves hold ordered data entries.

questions.prompt: Which operation in a B-tree handles a child that is full before insertion descends into it?
options: Convert the node into a stack
questions.explanation: Splitting prevents insertion into an overfull node.

questions.prompt: What is the asymptotic search cost in a B-tree with branching factor B and n keys?
options: O(1) comparisons and no node visits
questions.explanation: Large fanout reduces the height to logarithm base B.

questions.prompt: What does a leaf-level linked list in a B+ tree improve?
options: The ability to store unsorted pages only
questions.explanation: Linked leaves allow scanning adjacent key ranges without repeatedly returning to parents.

questions.prompt: Why are B-tree nodes kept partially full rather than exactly full after every update?
options: To allow efficient splits, merges, and future insertions
To make search linear in n
questions.explanation: Occupancy bounds balance space use and update cost.

questions.prompt: Which data structure is closer to write-optimized indexing than a classic in-place B-tree?
questions.explanation: Log-structured merge trees buffer writes and merge sorted runs.

questions.prompt: What problem does universal hashing try to reduce?
options: The height of an AVL tree
Adversarial collision patterns caused by predictable hash functions
The size of a stack frame
questions.explanation: Choosing from a hash family makes collisions harder to force.

questions.prompt: What is the key idea of Robin Hood hashing?
options: During insertion, keys with longer probe distances can steal slots from keys with shorter distances
Use a linked list for every character
Always store newest keys at the root
questions.explanation: Robin Hood hashing tries to equalize probe lengths.

questions.prompt: What is a cuckoo hashing insertion failure most likely to trigger?
options: Rehashing with new hash functions or a larger table
Ignoring the new key permanently as success
questions.explanation: Cuckoo insertion can cycle, so rebuilding may be needed.

questions.prompt: Why are tombstones problematic if never cleaned up in open addressing?
options: They turn the table into a complete binary tree
They make probe sequences longer even though entries were deleted
questions.explanation: Deleted markers still force searches to continue.

questions.prompt: What is perfect hashing designed to provide for a static key set?
options: No collisions for the stored keys
Automatic deletion of arbitrary future keys
questions.explanation: A perfect hash function maps each stored key to a unique slot.

questions.prompt: In extendible hashing, what does directory doubling respond to?
options: A bucket split that needs an additional hash prefix bit globally
questions.explanation: The directory grows when local depth exceeds global depth.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of using object identity hashing when logical equality is expected?
options: Equal-looking values may not be found because equality and hashing disagree
questions.explanation: Hashing must be consistent with the equality relation used for lookup.

questions.prompt: Which open-addressing scheme can fail to visit every slot if the step size and table size are not relatively prime?
questions.explanation: The probe step must cover the whole table to guarantee search of all slots.

questions.prompt: What is compressed sparse row format best suited for?
options: O(1) arbitrary edge deletion without moving data
Compact storage and fast scanning of neighbors in sparse static graphs
questions.explanation: CSR stores adjacency data in contiguous arrays with row offsets.

questions.prompt: Which data structure family can maintain dynamic forests with link and cut operations?
questions.explanation: Link-cut trees represent forest paths and support dynamic tree operations.

questions.prompt: What does heavy-light decomposition reduce path queries on a tree to?
options: One hash lookup with no preprocessing
A logarithmic number of contiguous base-array ranges
questions.explanation: Heavy paths map tree paths into a small number of array intervals.

questions.prompt: What is DSU with rollback designed to support?
options: Undoing union operations in offline algorithms
Permanent path compression only with no history
questions.explanation: Rollback DSU stores changes on a stack so unions can be undone.

questions.prompt: Why is full path compression usually avoided in rollback DSU?
options: It changes many parent pointers, making undo expensive
questions.explanation: Rollback works best when each union changes only a small recorded set of fields.

questions.prompt: What does an Euler tour tree represent?
options: A heap sorted by edge weights only
A dynamic forest using sequences of tree traversal occurrences
questions.explanation: Euler tour trees encode each tree as a sequence maintained by a balanced sequence structure.

questions.prompt: Which representation is efficient for iterating all edges sorted by source in a static sparse graph?
questions.explanation: CSR stores each vertex's neighbor range contiguously.

questions.prompt: What is the main operation supported by a lowest common ancestor structure built with Euler tour plus RMQ?
options: Answer LCA queries by reducing them to range minimum queries on depths
Hash arbitrary strings with no collisions
Delete graph edges online in O(1)
questions.explanation: The first occurrences in an Euler tour and minimum depth between them identify the LCA.

questions.prompt: Which operation is a classic limitation of a standard sparse table?
options: It cannot answer static idempotent range queries
It does not support efficient arbitrary updates after preprocessing
questions.explanation: Sparse tables are designed for static arrays.

questions.prompt: Why does RMQ with min work well with overlapping sparse table intervals?
options: min is idempotent, so overlapping elements do not affect correctness
questions.explanation: For idempotent operations, combining overlapping blocks is safe.

questions.prompt: What does a wavelet tree support efficiently?
options: Rank, select, and range quantile queries over sequences
questions.explanation: Wavelet trees recursively partition symbols and store bitvectors.

questions.prompt: What does a 2D Fenwick tree generalize?
options: Prefix aggregation over a two-dimensional grid
questions.explanation: It nests low-bit traversal in two dimensions.

questions.prompt: Which structure is suited to stabbing queries such as finding intervals containing a point?
questions.explanation: Interval trees augment nodes with endpoint summaries.

questions.prompt: What query is a kd-tree commonly used for?
options: Nearest-neighbor or orthogonal range search in low-dimensional space
questions.explanation: kd-trees recursively split points by coordinate axes.

questions.prompt: Why can kd-trees degrade in high dimensions?
options: They require all keys to be strings
Partition pruning becomes less effective as dimensionality grows
questions.explanation: The curse of dimensionality reduces pruning power.

questions.prompt: What does lazy propagation in a segment tree require for correctness?
options: Deferred tags must compose correctly with later updates and queries
Every node must be a hash bucket
Tags can be ignored after one query
questions.explanation: Incorrect tag composition yields wrong aggregates.

questions.prompt: What does a compressed trie, or radix tree, compress?
options: Every node into exactly two children
All keys into one hash value
Chains of single-child nodes into edge labels
questions.explanation: Compression reduces nodes when long paths have no branching.

questions.prompt: What is stored in a suffix array?
options: Starting positions of suffixes in lexicographic order
questions.explanation: A suffix array orders suffixes by their text content.

questions.prompt: What does the LCP array associated with a suffix array store?
options: Longest common prefix lengths of adjacent suffixes in suffix-array order
The last character of each suffix
The heap height of each suffix
questions.explanation: LCP captures shared prefixes between neighboring sorted suffixes.

questions.prompt: What is the role of failure links in the Aho-Corasick automaton?
options: They move to the longest proper suffix state that is also a prefix
questions.explanation: Failure links allow efficient multi-pattern matching after a mismatch.

questions.prompt: What does a suffix automaton compactly represent?
questions.explanation: A suffix automaton recognizes the set of substrings of the original string.

questions.prompt: Why do suffix trees often label edges by intervals into the original text?
options: To avoid storing copied substring labels explicitly
To sort suffixes by hash only
To force every edge label to length one
questions.explanation: Intervals represent substrings compactly.

questions.prompt: Which structure is appropriate for finding all dictionary patterns in a text in one pass?
questions.explanation: Aho-Corasick combines trie edges with failure links for multi-pattern search.

questions.prompt: What is a DAWG in string data structure terminology?
options: A doubly arrayed weighted graph only
A directed acyclic word graph representing substrings or a dictionary compactly
questions.explanation: DAWG commonly refers to a directed acyclic word graph.

questions.prompt: What kind of error can a standard Bloom filter produce?
options: False positives but not false negatives for inserted items
False negatives but not false positives
No error under any memory limit
Both false positives and false negatives always
questions.explanation: If an item was inserted, all its bits remain set unless deletions are unsupported and simulated incorrectly.

questions.prompt: What happens to Bloom filter false-positive probability as more items are inserted into a fixed-size filter?
questions.explanation: More set bits make accidental matches more likely.

questions.prompt: Why does a counting Bloom filter use counters instead of bits?
questions.explanation: Counters can be decremented when removing an item.

questions.prompt: What does a Count-Min Sketch estimate?
options: Approximate item frequencies with possible overestimation
questions.explanation: Collisions add counts, so estimates are never below true counts under standard assumptions.

questions.prompt: What does HyperLogLog estimate?
options: The parent of every heap node
questions.explanation: HyperLogLog uses hashed value patterns to estimate cardinality.

questions.prompt: In a skip list, what makes search expected O(log n)?
options: Search scans only the first node
The list is always a complete binary tree
Randomly chosen tower heights create logarithmic-level shortcuts
All nodes store the same height
questions.explanation: Higher levels let search skip over many bottom-level nodes.

questions.prompt: What advantage can a cuckoo filter have over a standard Bloom filter?
options: It has no false positives at any load
It stores all keys in sorted order
It can support deletion while still being compact
questions.explanation: Cuckoo filters store fingerprints in cuckoo hash tables and can delete entries.

questions.prompt: What is a quotient filter used for?
options: Approximate membership queries with compact hashed fingerprints
questions.explanation: Quotient filters are probabilistic membership structures.

questions.prompt: Why can an array-of-structures layout be slower than structure-of-arrays for scanning one field over many records?
options: It always has fewer cache misses
The needed field may be interleaved with unused fields, wasting cache bandwidth
questions.explanation: Structure-of-arrays groups each field contiguously, improving locality for column scans.

questions.prompt: What is false sharing in concurrent data structures?
options: Different threads update different variables that occupy the same cache line
Two keys share the same hash value only
Two tree nodes have the same parent
questions.explanation: Cache coherence can bounce the shared line even without logical sharing.

questions.prompt: What is the ABA problem in lock-free stacks?
options: A pointer changes from A to B and back to A, fooling a compare-and-swap
A hash table stores three equal keys
A binary tree has nodes named A and B
questions.explanation: CAS may see the same pointer value even though the structure changed.

questions.prompt: What do hazard pointers help with?
options: Safe memory reclamation in lock-free data structures
questions.explanation: Hazard pointers announce nodes that a thread may still access.

questions.prompt: What is an intrusive list advantage?
options: It stores nodes contiguously by definition
It forbids multiple lists per object always
It avoids separate allocation for list wrapper nodes
It turns list search into O(1) by value
questions.explanation: Links embedded in objects remove extra node allocation overhead.

questions.prompt: Why are memory pools often used for node-heavy data structures?
options: They eliminate all pointer bugs automatically
They reduce allocation overhead and improve locality
questions.explanation: Pools allocate many similarly sized nodes efficiently.

questions.prompt: What does RCU allow readers to do in some concurrent structures?
options: Read without taking heavy locks while updates publish new versions carefully
questions.explanation: Read-copy-update separates fast readers from synchronized updates and deferred reclamation.

questions.prompt: Which layout usually improves sequential traversal locality?
options: A hash table with one bucket per cache line always empty
Randomly allocated nodes connected by pointers
questions.explanation: Sequential memory access is cache- and prefetch-friendly.

questions.prompt: You need O(1) get, put, and recency update for an LRU cache. Which design is the classic choice?
options: Hash map from key to node plus doubly linked list of recency
questions.explanation: The map gives lookup, and the list moves nodes to most-recent position in O(1).

questions.prompt: You need delete(key), insert(key), getRandom(), all average O(1). Which core design works?
options: Binary search tree without augmentation only
Dynamic array plus hash map from key to array index
questions.explanation: The array supports random indexing, and the map supports location updates after swap-delete.

questions.prompt: You need O(1) increment/decrement string counts and retrieve any min or max key. Which idea is central?
options: A Bloom filter per count only
Buckets of equal counts linked in order plus key-to-bucket mapping
questions.explanation: The All O(1) design groups keys by count and moves them between adjacent buckets.

questions.prompt: Why is a hash map plus singly linked list insufficient for strict O(1) LRU eviction and arbitrary move-to-front?
options: Moving or deleting a known node needs predecessor access
Singly linked lists cannot store values
questions.explanation: A doubly linked list removes known nodes in O(1) without searching for predecessors.

questions.prompt: For a real-time system needing guaranteed O(log n) ordered map operations, which structure is safer than a splay tree?
options: Plain hash table with no ordering
questions.explanation: Splay trees are amortized, while AVL/RB trees provide worst-case logarithmic height.

questions.prompt: You need prefix count, exact word lookup, and delete for lowercase words. What should each trie node store at minimum beyond child links?
options: Counts or terminal markers that distinguish full words from mere prefixes
questions.explanation: Without terminal/count metadata, prefix paths cannot reliably identify complete stored words.

questions.prompt: Which pitfall breaks an ordered set implemented with a comparator?
options: The set has a root pointer
Comparator is not transitive or is inconsistent with equality
The set contains an odd number of elements
questions.explanation: Ordered trees require a strict weak ordering to place and find keys correctly.

questions.prompt: Why can storing mutable keys inside a hash set be dangerous?
options: The table immediately rehashes the key automatically in all languages
Mutating fields used by hash or equality can make the key unreachable in the table
questions.explanation: The key may remain in a bucket based on its old hash while lookup uses a new hash.

questions.prompt: Which standard header declares printf in C?

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a valid C identifier?
questions.explanation: C identifiers may contain letters, digits, and underscores, but cannot start with a digit.

questions.prompt: What is the result of 5 / 2 when both operands are of type int in C?
questions.explanation: Integer division discards the fractional part.

questions.prompt: What is the value of 17 % 5 in C?
questions.explanation: 17 divided by 5 leaves a remainder of 2.

questions.prompt: Which loop in C is guaranteed to execute its body at least once?
questions.explanation: A do-while loop checks its condition after executing the body.

questions.prompt: For int a[8]; what is the index of the last valid element?
questions.explanation: C arrays use zero-based indexing, so the last index is size minus one.

questions.prompt: A conventional C string is terminated by which character?
questions.explanation: C strings are arrays of char ending in the null character.

questions.prompt: Which keyword is used to define a structure type in C?
questions.explanation: C uses the struct keyword for structures.

questions.prompt: Which return type is used for a C function that does not return a value?
questions.explanation: The void return type indicates that no value is returned.

questions.prompt: Which statement exits the nearest loop or switch statement immediately?
questions.explanation: break transfers control out of the nearest enclosing loop or switch.

questions.prompt: Which statement skips the rest of the current loop iteration and continues with the next iteration?
questions.explanation: continue advances to the next iteration of the loop.

questions.prompt: Which scanf conversion specifier is used to read an int?
questions.explanation: %d reads a decimal int value.

questions.prompt: What is the usual return type of main in a hosted standard C program?
questions.explanation: In a hosted C environment, main returns int.

questions.prompt: Which expression is guaranteed by the C standard to have value 1?
questions.explanation: sizeof(char) is defined to be 1 byte in C.

questions.prompt: Which of the following starts a single-line comment in C99 and later?
questions.explanation: C99 introduced // single-line comments.

questions.prompt: Which operator checks equality in C?
questions.explanation: == compares two expressions for equality; = assigns.

questions.prompt: What is the default initial value of an object with static storage duration if no initializer is given?
questions.explanation: Objects with static storage duration are zero-initialized.

questions.prompt: What does #include commonly do during preprocessing?
options: Copies the contents of a header or source file into the translation unit
